questions.stem: The main role of the financial sector in the economy is to:
options: produce goods and services for households to buy and consume
collect taxes and redistribute income through transfer payments
set the prices of goods and services in competitive markets
channel funds from savers to borrowers who want to invest
questions.explanation: Financial institutions and markets move savings to households, businesses and governments that need funds, supporting investment and growth. Taxes and transfers are the role of government.

questions.stem: A financial intermediary is an institution that:
options: takes funds from savers and lends or invests them for borrowers
buys goods from producers and sells them on to consumers
regulates the conduct of companies listed on the stock exchange
prints notes and mints coins for use by the public
questions.explanation: Banks, insurers and fund managers stand between savers and borrowers, pooling funds and managing risk. Retailers buy and sell goods, and the RBA issues notes.

questions.stem: Which is a benefit of financial intermediaries to the economy?
options: They pool many small deposits to fund large loans and spread risk
They guarantee that every loan will be repaid in full and on time
They remove the need for households to save for the future
They set the cash rate to keep inflation within the target
questions.explanation: By pooling savings and diversifying loans, intermediaries make funds available for large projects and reduce risk for individual savers. The cash rate is set by the Reserve Bank, not commercial intermediaries.

questions.stem: Which institution is Australia's central bank?
options: The Australian Securities Exchange
The Australian Taxation Office
The Australian Office of Financial Management
The Reserve Bank of Australia
questions.explanation: The RBA conducts monetary policy, issues banknotes, oversees the payments system and acts as banker to the government. The ASX operates the main share market.

questions.stem: Insurers act as financial intermediaries because they:
options: lend deposits to households for mortgages and car loans
set the official interest rate for all financial institutions
buy and sell foreign currency on behalf of the government
invest the premiums they collect in shares and bonds
questions.explanation: Insurers collect premiums from many policyholders and invest them until claims must be paid, channelling savings into financial markets. Taking deposits and making mortgages is the main business of banks.

questions.stem: A fund manager is best described as an institution that:
options: insures households against losses from accidents and natural disasters
supervises the stability of banks, insurers and superannuation funds
pools money from many investors and invests it in a range of assets
accepts deposits and makes loans to households and businesses
questions.explanation: Fund managers, including managers of superannuation and managed funds, invest pooled money in shares, bonds, property and other assets. Supervising stability is the role of APRA.

questions.stem: Under Australia's superannuation guarantee, employers must:
options: pay employees' income tax directly to their superannuation fund
lend part of each employee's wage to the government each year
pay a set percentage of eligible employees' earnings into a super fund
match every dollar that employees choose to save in their bank account
questions.explanation: Compulsory employer contributions, in place since 1992, build retirement savings for most workers. The funds are invested by super funds until the member retires.

questions.stem: Superannuation is an important source of investment in the Australian economy because:
options: super funds lend directly to the Reserve Bank to fund its monetary policy operations
super funds spend members' contributions on consumer goods to support demand
super funds hold all members' savings as notes and coins in secure vaults
super funds invest a large pool of savings in shares, bonds and infrastructure
questions.explanation: Compulsory super has created one of the world's largest pools of retirement savings, providing a steady supply of funds for Australian and overseas investment. Funds are invested, not held as cash.

questions.stem: Which is a likely economic effect of compulsory superannuation?
options: Higher national saving and less reliance on the age pension in future
Lower national saving and more reliance on the age pension in future
Higher current consumption because workers no longer need to save
Lower investment because funds can only be invested overseas
questions.explanation: Compulsory contributions raise national saving and give more retirees their own income, reducing future pressure on the age pension. Super funds invest both in Australia and overseas.

questions.stem: An equity market is a market in which:
options: ownership shares in companies are issued and traded
governments and companies borrow by issuing bonds
currencies of different countries are exchanged
banks borrow and lend funds to each other overnight
questions.explanation: Buying shares gives the investor part-ownership of a company and a claim on its profits through dividends. Bonds are traded in debt markets.

questions.stem: A company lists on the Australian Securities Exchange and sells new shares to investors for the first time. This takes place in the:
options: foreign exchange market
primary share market
secondary share market
primary bond market
questions.explanation: The primary market is where new securities are issued and the company receives the funds. Later trading between investors occurs in the secondary market, and the company receives nothing from those trades.

questions.stem: Why is a liquid secondary share market important for the primary market?
options: Investors buy new shares more readily if they can easily sell them later
Companies receive the proceeds each time their shares are resold
Share prices in the secondary market are fixed by the government
It allows companies to borrow funds without paying any interest
questions.explanation: The ability to sell shares quickly at a market price reduces the risk of buying them, which makes it easier and cheaper for companies to raise new capital. Companies do not receive money from secondary trades.

questions.stem: Share prices on the secondary market rise strongly over a year. The most likely effect on the economy is that:
options: household wealth falls, reducing consumption, and firms find it harder to raise new capital
companies receive the gain in share value directly as extra revenue to spend on wages
interest rates on bonds automatically rise by the same percentage as share prices
household wealth rises, encouraging more consumption, and firms can raise capital more cheaply
questions.explanation: Higher share prices increase the wealth of shareholders, including super fund members, which can lift spending, and they let firms issue new shares on better terms. The gain goes to shareholders, not the company.

questions.stem: A payment of part of a company's profits to its shareholders is called:
options: a coupon
a premium
a yield curve
a dividend
questions.explanation: Dividends are the income return on shares. A coupon is the regular interest payment on a bond.

questions.stem: A bond is best described as:
options: an insurance policy that pays out if a borrower fails to repay a loan
a deposit held at a bank that can be withdrawn at any time on request
a debt security on which the issuer pays interest and repays the principal
a share that gives the holder part-ownership of a company and voting rights
questions.explanation: Bond holders are lenders, not owners: they receive regular interest (coupons) and their money back at maturity. Shares represent ownership.

questions.stem: The Australian Government sells newly issued Treasury bonds to investors at auction. This is a transaction in the:
options: secondary bond market
primary share market
secondary share market
primary bond market
questions.explanation: New government debt is issued in the primary market, raising funds for the government. Investors later trade those bonds among themselves in the secondary market.

questions.stem: A bond pays a fixed coupon of $50 a year. Market interest rates rise, so new bonds offer higher coupons. The price of the existing bond in the secondary market will most likely:
options: fall, so that its yield falls below new bonds
stay the same, since its coupon payment is fixed
fall, so that its yield rises to match new bonds
rise, so that its yield rises to match new bonds
questions.explanation: Investors will only buy the old bond if its price falls enough to give a yield similar to new bonds. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

questions.stem: Which is a key difference between equity and debt finance for a company?
options: Equity is available only to government enterprises, and debt only to firms
Debt must be repaid with interest; equity gives investors ownership instead
Equity must be repaid with interest; debt gives lenders ownership instead
Debt never has to be repaid, while equity must be repaid in full each year
questions.explanation: Borrowing creates an obligation to pay interest and repay principal regardless of profit, while selling shares gives up part of ownership and future profits. Both are used by private companies.

questions.stem: The interest rate can be described as:
options: the price of goods and services, measured by the CPI
the rate at which the population of a country grows
the share of income paid to the government in tax
the price of money, paid by borrowers and earned by savers
questions.explanation: Interest is the cost of borrowing and the return on saving, which is why interest rates influence both spending and saving. The CPI measures the price level.

questions.stem: A bank charges a well-established company 6% on a loan but charges a new business with no trading history 11%. The difference mainly reflects the role of interest rates as:
options: an indicator of risk
the return on savings
a measure of inflation
a tax on borrowing
questions.explanation: Lenders demand a higher rate from borrowers more likely to default, so interest rates signal risk. The return on savings is what depositors receive.

questions.stem: A rise in interest rates is most likely to affect households by:
options: lowering the cost of credit and raising the return on savings
raising the cost of credit and the return on savings
lowering the cost of credit and the return on savings
raising the cost of credit and lowering the return on savings
questions.explanation: Higher rates make loan repayments larger and deposits more rewarding, which encourages saving and discourages borrowing and spending. This is a key channel of monetary policy.

questions.stem: Which factor is most likely to increase the demand for loanable funds?
options: An increase in foreign investors' purchases of Australian bonds
A rise in business confidence and investment opportunities
A rise in household saving as people prepare for retirement
A fall in the number of profitable investment projects available
questions.explanation: When firms expect strong sales and profits, they want to borrow to invest. Higher saving and foreign purchases of bonds increase the supply of funds, not the demand.

questions.stem: Which factor would increase the supply of loanable funds in Australia?
options: A fall in domestic saving as households spend more of their income
A rise in foreign investment into Australian financial assets
A rise in consumer confidence leading households to borrow more
A large increase in government borrowing to fund a deficit
questions.explanation: Foreign investment adds to the funds available for lending in Australia. Consumer and government borrowing raise demand for funds, and lower saving reduces supply.

questions.stem: On a loanable funds graph, the demand for funds increases while supply is unchanged. The result is:
options: a lower interest rate and a larger quantity of funds borrowed
a higher interest rate and a smaller quantity of funds borrowed
a lower interest rate and a smaller quantity of funds borrowed
a higher interest rate and a larger quantity of funds borrowed
questions.explanation: A rightward shift in demand along an upward-sloping supply curve raises both the interest rate and the quantity of funds. The higher rate encourages more saving to meet the extra demand.

questions.stem: On a loanable funds graph, households increase their saving while demand for funds is unchanged. The most likely outcome is:
options: demand shifts left, the interest rate falls and fewer funds are borrowed
supply shifts right, the interest rate falls and more funds are borrowed
supply shifts left, the interest rate rises and fewer funds are borrowed
demand shifts right, the interest rate rises and more funds are borrowed
questions.explanation: More saving increases the supply of funds, pushing the interest rate down and encouraging more borrowing. Changes in saving shift the supply curve, not the demand curve.

questions.stem: The government runs a large budget deficit financed by borrowing. On the loanable funds graph, the main risk for private investment is that:
options: lower demand for funds lowers interest rates, reducing returns for savers
lower supply of funds raises interest rates, increasing household saving
higher demand for funds raises interest rates, crowding out private borrowing
higher supply of funds lowers interest rates, crowding in extra private borrowing
questions.explanation: Government borrowing adds to the demand for funds, which can push interest rates up and make some private projects unprofitable. This is known as crowding out.

questions.stem: Which government policy is most likely to increase the supply of funds?
options: Tax concessions that encourage households to save more
A first home buyer grant that increases mortgage borrowing
A larger budget deficit financed by issuing more bonds
Subsidies that encourage businesses to borrow and invest
questions.explanation: Encouraging saving adds to the funds available to lend. Grants that increase borrowing, larger deficits and investment subsidies all increase the demand for funds.

questions.stem: A rise in mortgage interest rates is most likely to affect a household with a variable-rate home loan by:
options: leaving its repayments unchanged until the loan is fully repaid
increasing its monthly repayments and reducing its disposable income
decreasing its monthly repayments and increasing its disposable income
reducing the amount it owes on the loan without any extra repayments
questions.explanation: Variable-rate repayments rise when lenders pass on higher rates, leaving less income for other spending. Fixed-rate borrowers are protected only until the fixed term ends.

questions.stem: Interest rates fall sharply. In the short term, the most likely effect on housing affordability for first home buyers is that:
options: borrowing capacity is unchanged, so house prices do not change at all
borrowing capacity rises, and house prices must fall by the same amount
borrowing capacity rises, but higher demand may push house prices up
borrowing capacity falls, so house prices fall and housing becomes cheaper
questions.explanation: Lower rates reduce repayments, so buyers can borrow more, but if many buyers bid more for a limited supply of homes, prices rise and offset part of the gain. Housing supply is relatively inelastic in the short run.

questions.stem: Rising interest rates are most likely to reduce housing affordability for new buyers mainly because:
options: deposits held in bank accounts lose value when rates rise
the same loan needs higher repayments, so buyers can borrow less
house prices always rise as soon as interest rates increase
the number of homes for sale is fixed by law when rates rise
questions.explanation: Lenders assess what borrowers can repay, so higher rates shrink how much they can borrow. Over time weaker demand may slow house price growth, partly offsetting the effect.

questions.stem: Which organisation operates Australia's main share market?
options: The Australian Taxation Office
The Australian Securities Exchange
The Reserve Bank of Australia
The Australian Prudential Regulation Authority
questions.explanation: The ASX runs the main market where listed companies' shares are issued and traded. APRA supervises the stability of banks, insurers and super funds.

questions.stem: Why might the Reserve Bank be described as a special kind of financial institution?
options: It manages the superannuation savings of most Australian employees
It sets monetary policy and is the banker to the government and to banks
It accepts deposits from households and makes loans to small businesses
It sells insurance policies and invests the premiums in shares and bonds
questions.explanation: The RBA does not lend to the public; it conducts monetary policy, holds accounts for banks and the government, and issues currency. Ordinary banks take deposits and lend.

questions.stem: A rise in household saving, with everything else unchanged, is most likely to:
options: reduce the supply of funds available for lending
raise interest rates charged on bank loans
increase the supply of funds available for lending
increase the demand for funds from borrowers
questions.explanation: Savings deposited with banks and invested through super and managed funds add to the pool of loanable funds. More supply tends to lower, not raise, interest rates.

questions.stem: Household confidence falls sharply and, at the same time, foreign investors pull funds out of Australia. On a loanable funds graph, the interest rate:
options: could rise or fall, because demand and supply of funds both fall
must rise, because demand and supply of funds both increase
must fall, because demand falls and supply of funds increases
must rise, because demand rises and supply of funds falls
questions.explanation: Lower confidence reduces demand for funds and capital outflow reduces supply. Both curves shift left, so the quantity of funds falls but the change in the interest rate depends on which shift is larger.

questions.stem: A $1,000 bond pays a coupon of $50 a year. In the secondary market its price falls to $800. Its yield to a new buyer is now about:
questions.explanation: Running yield = coupon / price = 50 / 800 = 6.25%. The coupon is fixed, so a lower price gives a buyer a higher yield; 5% is the yield at the original $1,000 price.

questions.stem: A business can earn a 7% return on a new project. Interest rates on business loans rise from 5% to 8%. In terms of the demand for funds, the most likely result is that:
options: the project is no longer worth borrowing for, so quantity of funds demanded falls
the project becomes more profitable, so quantity of funds demanded rises
the project is unaffected, because returns do not depend on interest costs
the business saves more, so the supply of funds in the economy falls
questions.explanation: Borrowing at 8% to earn 7% would lose money, so the firm drops the project. Higher interest rates reduce the quantity of funds demanded, a movement along the demand curve.
